### Why iterate? 

you will encounter problems where you need to wrtie the same basic code a lot  

### `for` loops 

loops are the easiest place to start: output object, sequence to iterate over, the loop body, and optionally an input object 
we might not use these loops for very long after learning them 

### Loop functions

loop process (supply input vector/list, apply function to each element, save the result to a vector/list) is very common 
for loops can get a little tedious and opaque --> loop functions clean this up. Use map functions

### map 

output = map(input, f) 
map across input, applying f function to each element, and spit out output 

### map variants 

by default, map takes one input and will return a list 
you can use specific map variants to help prevent errors and simplify outputs associated with what kind of output your function produces 

### workflow 

write single example for fixed inputs 
abstract example to a function 
(embed function in a loop) - can skip depending on how comfortable you are with map statement 
re-write using a map statement 

### Lists 

these provide a way to store collections of arbitrary size and type 
Can mix character vectors, numeric vectors, matrices, summaries 
Data frames are a special kind of list (each entry is a vector of same length. can still mix variable classes. printed as a table)

### list columns 

lists can contain anything, even another list --> this can be very useful in the context of iteration 
keeping everything in one dataframe with list columns means there are fewer things to worry about

## Lists 

Prove that lists can have anything 

```{r}
l = list(
  vec_numeric = 5:17, 
  mat = matrix(1:8, nrow = 2, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE), 
  vec_logical = c(TRUE), 
  summary_table = summary(rnorm(1000))
)

l 

l[[1]]

l[[2]]

l[["vec_logical"]]

l$summary_table #don't do this, shorthand for brackets 
```

# `for` loops 

```{r}
# create input list first 
list_norm = list(
  a = rnorm(20, 3, 4),
  b = rnorm(20, -14, 20),
  c = rnorm(20, 1000, 1000),
  d  = rnorm(20, 0, 1)
) 
```

Can I get mean and sd for each sample?
Use function we wrote last time 

```{r}
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[1]])
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[2]])
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[3]])
mean_and_sd(list_norm[[4]])

# pull out specific item in list, then apply that function 
# already tedious to deal with four of these --> write a for loop! 
```

Doing this better with a for loop: 

```{r}
#define an empty list for a space for each output I care about, length = 4 because we're working with four variables  
output = vector("list", length = 4) 

for (i in 1:4) { #go through 1, 2, 3, 4, put outputs of function on list norm into new list called output
  
  output[[i]] = mean_and_sd(list_norm[[i]])
  
}

output #empty list you made is now filled with the output from the for loop 
```

## use `map` instead

Take for loop and modify it 

```{r}
output = map(list_norm, mean_and_sd) #where we save output = (input list, function I care about)
output = map(list_norm, median) #can use map and change what function you apply 

#regular map always gives you a list 
```

## Map variants 

```{r}
output = map_df(list_norm, median) #simplifying outputs if you want, putting into df 

output = map_dbl(list_norm, median) #putting in a vector, doesn't separate out into list
```
